**Hydrogen – A Quick Reference Guide**

| Category | Property | Value / Description |
|----------|----------|---------------------|
| **Basic Identity** | Symbol | H |
| | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ |
| | Isotopes | H‑1 (protium), H‑2 (deuterium), H‑3 (tritium) |
| **Physical Properties (STP)** | State | Gas |
| | Color | Colorless |
| | Odor | Odorless |
| | Taste | Tasteless |
| | Density | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ (≈1/14 of air) |
| | Boiling point | –252.87 °C (120.95 K) |
| | Melting point | –259.16 °C (14.01 K) |
| | Specific heat (gas) | 28.836 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Molar volume | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ |
| | Compressibility factor (Z) | ~0.9 at 1 atm, 25 °C |
| **Chemical Properties** | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 |
| | Ionization energy | 13.598 eV |
| | Electron affinity | –0.754 eV |
| | Standard enthalpy of formation (ΔH°f) | 0 kJ mol⁻¹ (by definition) |
| | Standard Gibbs free energy of formation (ΔG°f) | 0 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Standard entropy (S°) | 130.68 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Oxidation states | +1 (as H⁺), –1 (as hydride H⁻) |
| | Common compounds | H₂O, H₂SO₄, H₂O₂, NH₃, CH₄, H₂O₂, etc. |
| | Reactivity | Highly flammable; reacts with O₂, N₂, Cl₂, metals (forming hydrides), acids (forming H₂ gas). |
| | Acid–base behavior | Acts as a weak acid (H⁺ donor) in aqueous solution; forms hydronium H₃O⁺. |
| | Redox behavior | Can be oxidized to H₂O or reduced to H₂ gas. |
| **Isotopic Variants** | Protium (¹H) | Stable, most abundant (~99.98 %) |
| | Deuterium (²H) | Stable, 0.015 % natural abundance; heavier, lower zero‑point energy |
| | Tritium (³H) | Radioactive (β⁻ decay, half‑life ≈12.32 y); used in nuclear fusion research and radiolabeling |
| **Nuclear Properties** | Nuclear spin | ½ (protium), 1 (deuterium), ½ (tritium) |
| | Magnetic moment | 2.7928 μ_N (protium), 0 (deuterium), 2.9785 μ_N (tritium) |
| | Binding energy per nucleon | ~1.1 MeV (protium), ~1.1 MeV (deuterium), ~1.1 MeV (tritium) |
| **Applications & Uses** | Energy carrier | Hydrogen fuel cells, rocket propellant (LH₂) |
| | Chemical industry | Production of ammonia (Haber process), methanol, hydrogenation reactions |
| | Materials science | Hydride formation, metal hydrides for storage |
| | Nuclear fusion | Deuterium–tritium fusion in experimental reactors |
| | Analytical chemistry | Isotope labeling, tracer studies |
| | Space exploration | Liquid hydrogen used as propellant for launch vehicles |
| **Safety & Handling** | Flammability range (air) | 4 % – 75 % (v/v) |
| | Explosion limit | 4 % (lower) – 75 % (upper) |
| | Health hazards | Inhalation of high concentrations can cause hypoxia; cryogenic burns from liquid H₂ |
| | Environmental impact | Low; produces only water vapor when combusted |

---

### Quick Takeaways

- **Hydrogen is the simplest element**: one proton, one electron, and (in its most common form) one neutron (protium).
- **It exists as a diatomic gas (H₂)** under normal conditions, but can also be found as a monatomic ion (H⁺) or hydride ion (H⁻) in various compounds.
- **Its isotopes** give it unique nuclear and chemical properties: deuterium is used in NMR and as a tracer; tritium is radioactive and central to fusion research.
- **Physically, it’s extremely light** and has the lowest boiling and melting points of all elements.
- **Chemically, it’s highly reactive** and serves as a key building block in countless industrial processes, from ammonia synthesis to fuel cells.

Feel free to ask if you’d like deeper details on any specific property or application!
